newsitem.title: USA: Three die, one missing in Texas floods.
newsitem.headline: Three die, one missing in Texas floods.

text.p: Three people died and one was missing in raging floodwaters that swept through central Texas following a weekend of heavy rains, officials said Monday.
Normally placid rivers in the Texas Hill Country became swollen torrents racing through limestone canyons after 21 inches of rain fell in some areas northwest of San Antonio.

Officials said the Llano River, 85 miles (136 km) north of San Antonio, had crested at 38.6 feet (11.6 meters), three times its normal floodstage and six feet (1.8 meters) above its highest level ever.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes throughout the region as lakes and rivers rose out of their banks. Television reports showed mobile homes swept from their foundations and floating in rapidly running waters.

Texas Division of Emergency Management spokeswoman Jo Schweikhard-Moss said rescuers pulled about 100 people from the floodwaters. "Many of them were caught when their houses were rapidly surrounded by water and they had no escape routes," she said.
Texas Department of Public Safety and National Guard helicopters were used to pluck people off roofs and from trees they grabbed to avoid being swept downstream.
Despite the rescue efforts, Schweikhard-Moss said two people in Bandera County, 50 miles (80 km) northwest of San Antonio, drowned when they lost their grip on trees before they could be saved.

A 12-year-old boy in the same county died in a weather-related traffic accident, while a man in Brown County, 150 miles (240 km) to the north, was missing after his car was swept away in high water, Schweikhard-Moss said.

At Johnson City, 65 miles (104 km) north of San Antonio, residents stood in awe of the Pedernales River, which runs in front of the ranch where the late President Lyndon Johnson lived. The usually small and shallow river was 25 feet (7.6 meters) above its banks and roaring so powerfully through the hills that clouds of spray hung above it.

"Normally out here a person is able to walk all the way across (the river) and visit some of the little pool areas. It's a leisurely flow of water. Right now, it's angry looking," said onlooker June Taylor.
Both the LLano and the Pedernales flow into the Colorado River, which rose rapidly through the weekend, flooding out a number of homes and businesses northwest of Austin, Schweikhard-Moss said.
